Mr. Speaker, I bow to your wishes, of course. I understand that some hon. members across the way blanch considerably at the mention of a government which is not prepared to borrow money to pay operating expenses. Perhaps I should go on to things less strange to them.
With respect to the problem concerning offshore resources, there are really two competing claims or philosophies which have been operating for many, many years. First, there is the federal authority which is based on the "authority in matters of trade and commerce" which is spelled out in the BNA Act. This conflicts directly with another item spelled out there whereby the provinces own their natural resources, which gives them a proprietary interest. I thought it might be of interest to hear what an expert in this field says. I refer to Dr. Bushnell of Windsor University. He says:
No one doubts that the provinces do own their natural resources-
This was before the parliamentary secretary made the opposite statement. However, Dr. Bushnell said at that time:
No one doubts that the provinces do own their natural resources (except for those which have been granted to private persons, and of course the granted resources could be acquired once again by the provinces), and that ownership rights allow the provinces to collect revenue.
What is the effect of this dichotomy between the provinces with their claim and the federal government with its claim? The provinces have power because they have the ability to determine the terms of leases and grants of mineral rights. The power of the federal government rests within the trade and commerce section of the BNA Act which permits it some pricing authority. There can be deadlocks, and there is one at present between Alberta and the federal government. The federal government has been gathering power in this area for several years, and quite a bit of it is due, of course, to the findings of the federal Supreme Court. Bushnell goes on to comment about this as follows:
In the interpretation of the trade and commerce power the Supreme Court has since 1957 expanded the Dominion's power from the attenuated position given it by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council... it would not seem feasible that the same Court, as long as a majority of the judges maintain the same interpretation of the trade and commerce power, would take with one hand and give back with the other by allowing proprietary rights to overcome the restriction on provincial power achieved through the trade and commerce power. Possibly allowing provincial control through the exercise of proprietary rights could be viewed as a compromise position, in that the exercise of proprietary rights has only the effect of nullifying the negative impact of the trade and commerce power and not the affirmative impact. Thus the provinces, through their proprietary rights, would be able to control natural resources in the absence of Dominion legislation. But in order to create that so-called compromise position the Court would have to give section 92(5) of the BNA Act an

July 14, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
interpretation which to date has not been given to any other provision in the Constitution. Section 92(5) would have to be interpreted to allow the province to legislate in relation to trade and commerce because it is dealing with provincially owned property.
The position of British Columbia is of course fairly well known. They were one of the later provinces to come into Confederation, and it is ridiculous to think they came in leaving their offshore behind- them belonging to some world power or something. They had the rights to the offshore before they joined Canada, and made a strong case in 1967, as mentioned by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). They lost that case in the Supreme Court of Canada. However, the B.C. court of appeals ruled that the waters and seabed of the Juan de Fuca Strait, Georgia Strait, Johnson Strait and Queen Charlotte Strait belonged to that province. I understand the federal government lodged an appeal in that case which has yet to be proceeded with.
Now, it might be of interest to examine the history of this dispute. One of the hon. members opposite claims there is something immoral about not accepting the Supreme Court decision, as though it were carved in stone. In 1978, at the first ministers' conference on the Constitution, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) accepted offshore resources as an item on the agenda for constitutional review at the behest of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. In February, 1979, at the first ministers' conference on the Constitution, the Prime Minister tabled a draft of the federal proposal that accepted the principle of concurrent legislative authority over offshore resources management.
A significant part of the judgment handed down in 1967 was that it applied only to British Columbia. However, the federal Department of Justice said the decision almost certainly means the BN A Act, the basis of the Canadian Constitution, will have to be amended before B.C. can gain offshore jurisdiction. Oil exploration off B.C.'s coast has shown little promise, but mining concerns have expressed interest in manganese nodules on the seabed floor.
It is obvious in following this that there is room for compromise. I feel quite certain that if the federal government were at all certain it has the right to these offshore resources, it would not be offering any kind of deal to a province. The smash and grab artists on the other side will give you absolutely nothing that they are not forced to give you. I think when they talk about a 75-25 split in the case of the Atlantic provinces, they are in fact admitting they have a very weak case.
What is needed is an honest, sincere look at the situation. We cannot go on with the stalemate between Alberta and the federal government. Other provinces do not wish to find themselves in a position where they have to exert their rights and harm other Canadians in order to protect their own interests. Yet this is what they are being forced to do by the abrasive Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that we can somehow or other come to an intelligent compromise where by the rights of the provinces will be respected, and we will get away from the
philosophy of the Minister of Justice that because they are so quick to take more money which belongs to other people.

Well, they are going to spill a lot of it, I tell you. What is the parallel here to Saskatchewan and Alberta? The whole energy policy is designed along the direction laid in Bill C-48. Investigate this closely as in the coming days we will be relating it to how the government is seeking to nationalize the oil industry, and you will see that never before has a bill been brought before this House which has taken such great steps to nationalize the oil industry as does this bill before us. Through Petro-Canada, the government takes 25 per cent of all existing oil resources in the Canada lands, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. All that has to happen is for that percentage to change from 25 to 50 to 75, and you have a nationalized oil industry in Canada.
I want to say without equivocation: this policy is not going to work. It is going to have repercussions which we in western Canada have already felt very severely. What have those repercussions been? We have driven out 170 oil rigs. The independent oil people tell us that they believe we will lose half the fleet or 250 oil rigs. The energy policy has driven out 85 service rigs and along with the oil rigs and the service rigs,
July 14, 1981

many winch trucks, caterpillars and other related heavy equipment. What has the loss been to Canada? We have suffered a tremendous economic loss under this energy policy. We in the Conservative party view Canada as a great chain and each province as a link. I am very pleased to have 20 minutes to speak on motion No. 3. I believe it is the key motion which is before us. More than that, I think it is what differentiates this government from the opposition, the Tory Party in particular, and surprisingly enough from the New Democratic Party.
What we are really talking about on this side of the House is a bill which defines what is a nation. What is being talked about on the opposite side of the House is the whittling away of a nation so that there is nothing left.
Let us look at the motion which is before us, since it is a very interesting one. The Chair has just read the gist of the motion. It would remove Sable Island from the definition of Canada lands. That is the first thing it does. Let us consider Sable Island for a moment. The first time I saw mention of Sable Island was in Article 91.9 of the British North America Act, where the island is included under the powers of the Parliament of Canada. What we are trying to do is to amend the British North America Act. We are taking something in the British North America Act and saying that it is no longer there; it is not part of Canada lands.
I am not a lawyer and I do not want to spend a lot of time on this side of the situation, Mr. Speaker, but in the British Columbia case which dealt with who owns the territorial waters and the continental shelf, the province of British Columbia or the federal government, the most obvious reason that the British Columbia claim did not hold up was that the matter was not covered in Section 92 of the British North America Act.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
As I recall my history, when the Fathers of Confederation were setting up this country, they had an image of what was across the border that scared them. One of the reasons this country was put together was the possibility of attack from across the border. When they wrote the British North America Act, which was later passed by the government of Great Britain, they were interested in setting up something which was much stronger. Unfortunately, members of the Tory party today forget that it was our first prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, who wanted a very strong nation.
One of the things that the Fathers of Confederation did was to leave in the hands of Parliament those things that were not enumerated.
In many ways, we are trying to take away from the British North America Act something which I think all of us believe only the British Parliament can do. I will grant, Mr. Speaker, that there is a considerable difference in the case of Newfoundland. There is no question about that. In the case of British Columbia and the other territorial waters off, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, jurisdiction was just to the edge of the ocean. Anything east of the Pacific Ocean was in the province of British Columbia, up to the border of British Columbia. It was the same with the other provinces. In the case of Newfoundland we are dealing with quite a different concept and I will not go into it now. I certainly will not get into the question of international waters.
Since I have the floor, Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate it if I could carry on a monologue.
I should like to make the point that we have the Geneva agreement and we have treaties. We are talking about the 200-mile continental shelf which permits only the state, that is, Canada, to exploit land in that continental shelf or beyond the 12-mile limit of what is known as the territorial ocean.
How, as a self-respecting nation which belongs to the summit group and which is hosting a meeting of the most powerful non-communist states in the world next week, can we say that we are no longer in control of that area but that the provinces have control of it? I do not understand this.
I do not understand how the two opposition parties can put themselves in the position where they want to change the British North America Act right in this House. They do not even want to ask Britain to do it. After all the fuss the Tories made about going to Britain or even going to the courts to find out whether we could do it, we are saying that Sable island is no longer part of the Canada land. But there it is, in Section 91(9), Sable Island. Section 92 does not mention the offshore or territorial waters, so clearly under the British North America Act it is within the realm of the Parliament of Canada. Are we to accomplish this by just changing one act?
There is nothing to stop us from doing it, Mr. Speaker. But there is a very serious question about whether it would have any relevance. We can always make laws that contravene the British North America Act, but of course the courts would not sustain them.

I think this is important and I think it should be remembered, particularly by the NDP. There are many stories about this kind of manipulation in states such as Oklahoma and Texas, and it was a major factor in the whole offshore fight.

The hon. member for St. John's East replied that I was being patronizing, or something to that effect. He can correct me if I am not telling the story properly. I thought about northern Ontario where I come from. Precisely the same thing has happened to us in northern Ontario, a weak but large part of our province. We are virtually treeless now, or will be treeless if we do not do something very quickly, because the province of Ontario has been manipulated by a large number of paper companies over the long term. Basically we are now in a position where the economy of the north is in serious jeopardy. It is much better at this stage that we as a nation share in these resources. We should share the revenues with those parts of the country which have the resources. However, the ownership or control of these kinds of resources and the resources in those areas which would be excluded by this motion must remain in the hands of the federal government, from the international point
of view, the British North America Act and the equity of the whole country.
The people of Canada should understand the meaning of this motion. Mr. Speaker, I have to admit that this has been a spellbinding debate. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) and the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) certainly have rare gifts and unique views of the universe, and certainly opposite.
Tonight I want to deal with something which fits directly into my riding. The area off the west coast that is seriously being considered affects directly Comox-Powell River. The shallow basin that exists there has an estimated 300 million to four billion barrels of oil, and maybe as much as 90 trillion cubic feet of gas. That sits right off my riding in Queen Charlotte Sound, Hecate Strait, Johnstone Strait and off the west coast of the island. Motion No. 3 deals with the definition of Canada lands. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon certainly are lands that belong to the Government of Canada as well as the offshore area in the Arctic.
These, however, are not clearly Canada lands. There are other claims, such as aboriginal claims of peoples who were here before the tenure was decided. Those questions must be decided. Ownership of the oil and gas in those lands are called into question. This provision deals with it before those claims have been dealt with. I suggest that removal before dealing with those questions could be removing somebody else's property, and that should be effectively dealt with.
I now want to deal with the other submarine areas adjacent to the two coasts, British Columbia and areas off the Atlantic coast. I understand this motion would advocate that we delete Sable Island and the adjacent submarine areas. That makes sense, but certainly from very different points of view than those raised by members opposite and members to my right.
The two basic questions we face in this bill is, first, that the federal government advocates total jurisdiction. The second major issue, and it has been raised effectively by my colleagues to the right, is the question of tremendous discretionary power in the hands of the minister.
The basic question is: should the federal government have complete jurisdiction over development of oil and gas in offshore areas adjacent to the provinces? I feel, as do a lot of others, that the answer to that question is no. Bill C-48 gives the federal government total jurisdiction and gives the minister unfettered discretionary power. The minister continually justified that in committee saying, we really do not know what is going to happen, we want a free hand". Over the period of history of oil and gas in Canada, no one can dispute that.
July 14, 1981

The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan and many others have said that the oil companies have taken us to the cleaners many times and the federal government was in power during that period of time. We find that in this bill there is no clear statement of what the goals should be. The minister and others responsible should have clear instructions to move effectively toward the goals we want to achieve.
We have a bill which moves for complete jurisdiction in areas that have a long history of control over their internal economies and their resources. 1 suggest that the arguments the government members have put forward are very weak. In fact, they miss the point.
The government members have said we need this power and this control, that in order to keep Canada together we must have energy self-sufficiency, and we have to ensure adequacy of supply and fairness of access. They have also said that they want a share of the revenue in that endeavour. They believe that across Canada there should be an equalization of opportunities for Canadian citizens, that health care, education and the basic expectations of Canadian citizens have to be met and, therefore, that is a source of revenue that should be shared.
Basically there are two points, the energy security and access question and the sharing of revenue. Those goals are correct, but this bill is not the mechanism. We already have mechanisms in place giving complete jurisdiction to the federal government, and to give the minister unfettered discretionary power, and does this bill, without laying out clearly the goals and how he is to achieve them, will create a serious problem.
I suggest this massive appeal to Canada as a nation that it will somehow be destroyed if the provinces are given an effective say in resource development and development of their local economies is a false argument. If we in British Columbia control our resources and resource development, it does not mean that Canada will suffer. There is already the National Energy Board Act and other legislation which governs how energy resources are to be allocated in this country. There is the Income Tax Act and other provisions by which revenue can be taken and dispersed in order to ensure equalization and fair opportunity. It is basically wrong to prohibit those long-standing coastal states from having a meaningful share in the say with regard to development of their resources.
The other side of the coin has been the very compelling and persuasive arguments from my colleagues to the right who say there should be total provincial control over those resources. It is interesting when we look at the dilemma. In the case of British Columbia, over the years there has been the development of oil and gas by multinational corporations, corporations with budgets and financial influence greater than this country. They have not served the best interests of this country. They have largely been let lose by this Liberal government to do their deeds. It will be an interesting and difficult problem to be solved for those multinationals, both the Canadian and foreign owned ones.
The first prime minister of this country presided over what was called the Liberal-Conservative party. That party built an
Canada Oil and Gas Act
organization in the 1880s called the Canadian Pacific Railroad which ripped off this country from stem to stern. There was a combination of the Liberal-Conservative party, the Bank of Montreal and the Canadian Pacific Railroad. We still have not recovered from that rip-off.
In the 1980s we are creating another CPR out of Dome Petroleum, almost the same mechanism. We will have a very large multinational corporation within Canada. That is not the key point in this. The problem is that those large corporations in provinces like British Columbia and areas like the maritime provinces will be able to whipsaw, thus causing enormous problems. The whole business of corporate blackmail over a period of time has been a problem. What we would find with total provincial control is manipulation of those provincial governments with economic power and clout that would be difficult to resist. So total controls may not be the answer. There is another thing to consider in my area.

speechtext:
Be very careful and read the resolution to the end. Maybe by the end of the presentation I will be able to develop the total concept.
In British Columbia we have had a very interesting small group of people who have capitalized on an enormous amount of economic development in that province. Throughout my area, where much of this offshore drilling and development should take place, there are small communities which have been left out of the mainstream of economic development throughout the history of that province. They are left out today, and when the oil and gas in their communities is developed and removed, they will still be left out because there is a small group of individuals who tend to capitalize on the economic opportunities to reap the benefits. If we look to the east coast, we recognize those names today, whether it is in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Newfoundland. In those areas they are in position and working. In British Columbia there is clear evidence that they are mobilizing, and the government of British Columbia and the Liberal government in Ottawa have done nothing to make sure those other communities participate in the economic benefits.
The whole question of total provincial control means that multinationals would have a very large say, with possibly whipsaw and cost problems. There are local oligarchies which have always benefited at the expense of many other segments in those provincial societies. They would tend to work with those multinationals to benefit.
There is also the question of federal resources. If in fact an oil spill should occur off Rivers Inlet, Calvert Island, Bella Bella, northern Vancouver Island-wherever it happens to occur-such as the one that took place in the Caribbean that cost $1 billion to cap, the province of British Columbia is not going to cap that; it is not going to clean it up. It will require the resources of the federal government. If you have to take responsibility for long-term consequences, there is a question

July 14, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
of resources. I am convinced, after listening to testimony, that we are not talking about the possibility of an oil spill occurring, we are talking about the timing of such an oil spill. Whose resources will pay for cleaning it up and who is going to have a say in the standards? I would urge my colleagues to the right to consider that maybe total provincial control needs better definition; maybe it needs some slight change.
The last thing we have to take a serious look at is the whole question of some very deep rooted economic disparities. Total provincial control has never been able to address this in the past. With the opportunity to develop this oil and gas, I doubt whether we will be able to see, with control in provincial hands, the removal of disparity among some of those communities. Possibly in terms of provincial control we have to look to a different mechanism.
On the other side of the coin of provincial control, we have a couple of items. First of all, decisions should be left as much as possible in the hands of the people whom those decisions affect-local communities and regional areas. They have the right to make the decisions that affect their lives. The argument for provincial control is sound in that respect. Local authorities with an opportunity to develop those resources would be more accountable. There is no doubt that a politician in British Columbia, or a government there or in Nova Scotia is more accountable to the people than a government in Ottawa. There are as many members of Parliament from the greater Toronto area as there are from the entire province of British Columbia. When you address a question from British Columbia to central Canada, or the Parliament of Canada, it is diluted down a tremendous degree. National priorities are far higher than local or regional priorities.
Therefore, as my colleagues on the right I think correctly pointed out, local control is imperative. Local control would have an opportunity to be more accountable to the needs of the people, whether they are associated with the disparity question, a response to environment or the strengthening of small economies. If you give control of oil development to the provinces, the local or regional areas, you will strengthen those communities in my area. You will provide more improved transportation. We have sat in this House and battled for years over improved transportation. If those communities on the coast of B.C. had improved transportation, their entire economic development, their stake and their position would improve, but this falls on deaf ears in this House. Maybe if this oil is developed under local control, the transportation system will improve and develop. We would then wind up with strengthened communities and improved transportation systems, and, by and large I think an improved situation.
We have a strange dichotomy here. We have the Tories on the right arguing for total provincial control and we have the Liberals with national interest in equalization and, basically, an energy security structure, arguing for federal control. Maybe the ultimate solution is a new approach, one that says there should be co-operative development of those resources, and that as much as possible the federal government should set standards for the development and define, in agreement with
the provinces, where development can occur. If the provinces were in a position to meet those agreements, those minimum standards, they could develop and improve beyond that in ways that would be meaningful to those people. What we will wind up with is maybe a new approach, maybe one which says that the federal government should sit down with the province of British Columbia and discuss what offshore oil and gas development could mean to that province and where there could be a meeting of minds. Possibly there should be the passing of reciprocal legislation to give momentum to that kind of agreement.
Then beyond that point possibly British Columbia, in agreement with the federal government, could take control of developing an area, which is really developing resources that are within the confines of the province of British Columbia, in Hecate Strait, Queen Charlotte Sound or in Johnstone Strait, and in that way maybe we could deal with both aspirations- with the question of equalization and resource sharing. In this way we could settle the question of control over those resources in order to provide security on a national basis, as well as provide tremendous local benefits by giving British Columbians an opportunity to say how local communities will be strengthened as a result of the development and how transportation should be improved.
We could also decide how to remove pockets of deep-seated and chronic disparity such as exists in the Indian communities. Under the present system they will receive the oil spills and probably the negative effects of such development. VETERANS AFFAIRS-(A) APPOINTMENT OF FULLTIME MINISTER. (B) DECENTRALIZATION OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 23 of this year I directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding the appointment of a fulltime Minister of Veterans Affairs. In the Department of Veterans Affairs today we have a very serious problem regarding the processing of veterans' pension applications, some of which take from one to five years to process. I pointed out at the time that the present minister has not been able to find a
July 14, 1981

solution to the problem. I asked that the Prime Minister inform us when he would be appointing a full-time minister who can deal with this very serious problem in the department. We received one of the evasive and uninformative answers we usually receive from the Prime Minister, regardless of whatever question we are posing to him.
I also asked the Prime Minister whether the government would be considering leaving the Pension Commission in Ottawa in order to rectify the one to five years' delay in processing veterans' pension applications. We received some more typical Liberal gobbledygook on that.
At a recent meeting of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs the chairman of the Pension Commission pointed out that he has very, very serious problems finding personnel who wish to transfer to Prince Edward Island and, of course, this is delaying the processing of veterans' pension applications.
Speaking in the House on July 10 of this year with regard to Bill C-82, which was amendments to the Pension Act and the Compensation for Former Prisons of War Act, the acting Minister of Veterans Affairs pointed out:
-I am confident this legislation will have the support of all parties. It is further proof of this nation's resolve that veterans and their survivors will continue to receive just and generous treatment.
At the present time, veterans are not receiving just and generous treatment if they have to wait up to five years to have their pensions processed, and we have a serious problem with respect to a very high percentage of veterans passing on before their applications can be processed. I have called this before an absolute national disgrace.
Because I received no firm or concrete answers from the Prime Minister to my questions to him, I wrote him a letter with respect to this problem, and I understand that officials in the Pension Commission and in the Department of Veterans Affairs are in the process of compiling an answer to my letter.
The letter I wrote to the Prime Minister was dated June 25, and I called for the appointment of a full-time minister of veterans affairs. I also pointed out that there are two main factors causing a malaise within the department. In the first instance, the legislation which the department has to deal with is cumbersome and archaic. As the chairman of the Pension Commission has pointed out in the Standing Committee of Veterans Affairs, he is hamstrung with the present legislation. There is no way he can process veterans' pension applications any quicker. It will take from one to five years under the present legislation. That is why I am on my feet tonight. I am on my feet to request once again that a new piece of legislation be introduced as soon as possible to cut out all this rigmarole veterans have to go through before pension applications can be processed.
I will give hon. members the exact wording of what we heard from Mr. Solomon in the standing committee on May 28. Mr. Solomon stated:
These procedures-
Adjournment Debate
Referring to the Canadian legislation.
-although they are marvelous safeguards, take time, and they are hamstringing us in many ways.
In my letter to the Prime Minister I said that the aging veterans in this country simply do not have the years left to wait for this hamstringing, time-consuming legislative process to run its course.
In a letter dated June 2 of 1980 Mr. Chadderton, the chief executive officer of the War Amputations of Canada, listed the names of some 370 veterans associated with that organization alone who died waiting for their pensions. The War Amps are dealing with this figure in gathering detailed statistical information which is required before it can make applications to the Pension Commission. This figure is in addition to the applications the Pension Commission already has in hand.
I understand the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs is going around privately challenging these figures. I understand there are phone calls going on at the present time challenging the figures; it is not 50 per cent, it is some other figure. That is not the point at all, Mr. Speaker. We need a piece of legislation to get rid of this archaic nonsense of taking up to five years to process a veteran's application. That is the point, not whether it is 40, 50 or 60 per cent.
I have gone into great detail in my letter to the Prime Minister with regard to actual individual cases which have come to my attention. Every day there is a member of the Conservative party who comes to me and says: What are we going to do about the Pension Commission? What are we going to do about getting these applications processed? That is all I have listened to since I have been the spokesman for the Conservative party on veterans affairs. We have evasive answers from the acting minister. He has absolutely nothing to say, and tries to slough it all off on his officials. We are getting absolutely nowhere. Some of the Liberals are laughing; it is a big joke with them.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-(A) APPOINTMENT OF FULLTIME MINISTER. (B) DECENTRALIZATION OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) comes to the House with an argument short on facts and long on fiction.
I want to deal with the two points he raised in a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on June 23 as reported at page 10885 of Hansard.
The hon. member asked the Prime Minister when he would appoint a minister of veterans affairs, and if he would consider having the headquarters of the Canadian Pension Commission stay in Ottawa and not relocate to Prince Edward Island.
Since the death of the Hon. Daniel MacDonald, Mr. Speaker, the acting Minister of Veterans Affairs has been responsible before Parliament for the portfolio. In this House, before its committees and the committees of the other place, the acting minister, being himself a veteran and a former POW, has been a stalwart representative of the interests of veterans and their families. The Prime Minister, when answering the

July 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
member, took the opportunity to state once again his intention of appointing a minister. Hon. members will recall the previous government had designated one minister to be permanently responsible for Veterans Affairs and National Defence. This was done in spite of and in complete disregard of the wishes of veterans as expressed in the vigorous campaign mounted by the Royal Canadian Legion.
So for the hon. member to come here this evening and berate the government and the Prime Minister for not appointing a full-time minister immediately when his own government had put the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) permanently in charge of both National Defence and Veterans Affairs, I think is completely incongruous.
In addition, the relocation of the veterans affairs head office to Charlottetown was announced on October 26, 1976. The decision applied to the department and the four agencies, and was part of the government's policy of decentralization whose goals were: To move the administration of federal government programs closer to the people directly affected by them; to increase the presence of the federal government in communities where it has been low and where activities of a national nature can contribute to national unity; and to reduce the disproportionately high concentration of federal employees in the national capital region.
The relocation of Veterans Affairs involves the transfer of some 760 positions to Charlottetown of which 271 are with the Canadian Pension Commission. Presently, there are 160 DVA employees working in Charlottetown. The number of employees who agree to move will not be known until nine months prior to the official date of relocation of the positions. At present, the expected date of relocation for the Canadian Pension Commission is September, 1983.
The relocation has received the approval of three governments including the previous one, and I can assure the House that every effort is being made to minimize any disruption in the service provided to veterans. We are confident that veterans and their families will be as well served by departmental and agency employees working from Charlottetown as they were from Ottawa.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg Assiniboine is inflaming passions with statements not based on fact but based on his own great imagination.

COMBINES-REQUEST FOR RELEASE OF REPORT ON URANIUM CARTEL. (A) REQUEST THAT INDEPENDENT PROSECUTOR REVIEW EVIDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight with respect to the persistent questioning of the government by members of my party concerning the uranium cartel and the subsequent charges which have been laid respecting a number of companies in Canada including Crown corporations within which two senior government officials
were named in the information as unindicted co-conspirators, namely, Mr. MacNabb and John Runnalls.
Our inquiries with respect to the uranium cartel activities have, to a large extent, been directed toward the whole concept of determining whether or not the government has any understanding at all of the traditional parliamentary concept of ministerial responsibility. The government has consistently refused, in answering questions on the floor of the House of Commons and outside the House, to say whether Messrs. MacNabb and Runnalls acted on their own or on the instruction of the government. It is a rather peculiar evasion of a very essential and important fact respecting this matter.
It went to the extent that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) would not even tell us whether the government was prepared to provide counsel for these two people in the course of the legal proceedings which are about to take place in the prosecution.
Mr. Donald Macdonald was the minister during a good portion of time during which, the allegation is made in the information, there was a price-fixing arrangement respecting domestic prices in Canada. Mr. Macdonald indicated the following in a CBC interview:
I can certainly say that there is absolutely no indication at any point to myself and I am sure other federal officials that the companies were getting together to take advantage of the situation-
Also he indicated that no one at the federal level was consulted about domestic prices following world prices. But there are a number of instances which are now a matter of public record that fly in the face of this contention on the part of Mr. Macdonald and of the response of the government. First, the Gulf memorandum of March 8, 1974 clearly indicated that the officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources recognized that Canadian utilities must be prepared to pay export prices. Second, the companies themselves were initially very concerned about the combines law. Third, apparently cabinet discussed the possible domestic consequences of the cartel at the outset of the arrangement. Fourth, we have the simple and bald fact that Messrs. MacNabb and Runnalls are now named as co-conspirators.
I will not comment on whether or not any further charges should be laid. It is really impossible to tell. That is the reason we are trying to get more information as to why a greater number of people who were clearly involved in the cartel arrangement were not joined, even as unindicted co-conspirators, or named in the information.
Officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources were involved. Either the minister knew what was happening at the time or he was ignorant. In either event, there are serious problems. The government is attempting to reduce the issue to a narrow legal one and trying to escape any further questioning on the basis that the matter is now before the court.
The principle of ministerial responsibility is basic and goes beyond the technical, legal culpability. This has nothing to do with the notion which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advanced in the House that you must trust somebody.
July 14, 1981

I should like to refer to the fifth edition of "The Government of Canada" by R. MacGregor Dawson and revised by Norman Ward of Saskatoon. Page 176 of the book reads as follows:
The minister at the head of every department is responsible for everything that is done within that department; and inasmuch as he will expect praise or assume blame for all the acts of his subordinates, he must have the final word in any important decision that is taken.
It continues:
R. L. Borden, when leader of the opposition, aptly described the ideal situation as follows:
A Minister of the Crown is responsible, under the system in Great Britain, for the minutest details of the administration in his department; he is politically responsible, but he does not know anything at all about them. When anything goes wrong in his department, he is responsible therefore to Parliament; and if he comes to Parliament and points out that he entrusted the duty to an official in the ordinary course and in good faith, that he had been selected for his capacity, and ability and integrity, and the moment that man had gone wrong the Minister had investigated the matter to the full and punished that man either by degradation or dismissal, he has done his duty to the public. That is the way matters are dealt with in Great Britain, and it is in that way, it seems to me, that our affairs ought to be carried on in this country.
Mr. Macdonald, the minister in 1972 and 1975, was interviewed by the CBC yesterday morning in Edmonton. In the course of that interview, he was asked by the interviewer whether at any time the reports which Crown corporations had to make to government involved the price being charged for uranium on the domestic market. In his response, Mr. Macdonald said in part:
No, 1 don't think so any more than the kind of conduct ... by CBC employees should be a matter of day to day surveillance by ministers-
The interviewer interrupted, but Mr. Macdonald went on to
say:
Just let me finish, please, you can trust the operations of the Crown corporations to officials to whom you have confidence and that was done and the question has now been raised by the Combines people as to whether or not the management of those two corporations exceeded the law in what they did.
In reviewing the annual reports of Uranium Canada, which is a Crown corporation, I find it peculiar when looking through the reports from 1972 to the present time to find out exactly what is reported to the minister. This is a Crown corporation of which Mr. Runnalls and Mr. MacNabb were officers.
I wish to make two observations. The first is that Uranium Canada had no personnel and that the administration of that corporation was carried out exclusively by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. There were no employees of Uranium Canada. Who were the officers of Uranium Canada from 1972 to 1975? The president was one Jacob Austin, otherwise known as Jack Austin, otherwise known as Senator Jack Austin. In one of his aliases, he was deputy minister to the minister of energy, mines and resources and, in fact-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the two questions raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn). The first question is a request for the release of the report on uranium cartel.
Adjournment Debate
On September 30, 1977, the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), made an order pursuant to paragraph 8(c) of the Combines Investigation Act requiring the Director of Investigation and Research to inquire into the marketing of uranium with a view to obtaining all the facts and determining whether a violation of the Combines Investigation Act had occurred. In other words, the Director of Investigation and Research was required to conduct an investigation into the question of whether any individual or corporation had committed an offence. The Director carried out the investigation, and then on May 25, 1981, a report on the evidence gathered was submitted to the Attorney General of Canada pursuant to section 15 of the Combines Investigation Act in order to enable the Attorney General to decide what course should be followed.
It has always been the policy of the Department of Justice not to release reports made to it on investigations conducted into the commission of alleged offences. This applies whether the investigation relates to alleged violations of the Combines Investigation Act, the Income Tax Act, the Narcotic Control Act, the Customs Act and so on. The reason for the policy is simply based on considerations of fair play. If the person or corporation who has been investigated is not charged, to release the report on the investigation could very well amount to publicly accusing him of violating the law without the person concerned having any opportunity to defend himself or herself. On the other hand, if a charge is laid, then the results of the investigation are made public under the circumstances which are controlled by a court of law. That is to say, the evidence that is submitted must be admissible evidence and the accused person must be given an opportunity to make full answer and defence. I repeat, this has always been the policy of the Department of Justice and, as indicated, is based on considerations of fair play and natural justice.
The second question is a request that an independent prosecutor be appointed to review the evidence. When the Director of Investigation and Research commenced his inquiry, he-not the government or any member of the government-chose Mr. John Brown of the Toronto firm of Blake, Cassells and Graydon in September of 1977 to assist him in the inquiry. After working on the case for over three years, Mr. Brown reported his conclusions to the Director of Investigation and Research in April of this year. As already indicated, the director, in turn, referred the case to the Attorney General of Canada last May. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) sought further direct advice from Mr. Brown on the question of whether prosecution was warranted. He was advised in the affirmative and Mr. Brown has been appointed agent of the Attorney General of Canada and special prosecutor on the case.
There is absolutely nothing upon which to base any suggestion that Mr. Brown has acted throughout other than in a capacity totally independent of influence from the government. Indeed, any suggestion of that kind would simply be an unwarranted and unfounded reflection on Mr. Brown's profes-

July 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
sional integrity. For these reasons there is no basis for a request that yet another independent counsel be appointed to review the evidence.

BANK ACT-QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE REVISIONS TO CONTROL INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to protest the answers to questions about interest rates given in this House, in light of the statements on the same subject made outside the House. There seems to be some discrepancy between what is said in the House and what pass for answers outside the House.
It all began when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was quoted in the press. This is only one quote from many speeches delivered around the farming community this spring. In the Western Producer of May 14, 1981, there appears the following:
During his Humboldt address, Whelan also severely criticized the banks for showing what he called their lack of responsibility toward the problems farmers are now facing with high interest rates.
The article goes on:
Whelan added it was "criminal" that efficient producers are going bankrupt over high rates.
Earlier the same article had this to say:
Whelan said he will try to get the amendment into the Bank Act during the current review of the act.
The Bank Act was dealt with seven or eight months prior to that time, Mr. Speaker. When the question concerning the statements of the Minister of Agriculture was raised in the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) replied that he believed that the matter was clarified the previous week in the House when the Minister of Agriculture acknowledged that he did not have in mind the revision of the Bank Act. He added that he did not have that in mind either. That should have put an end to the doubt about the government's policy with regard to interest rates. We know from experience that the Minister of Agriculture quite often engages in flights of fancy. He is well known to be an expert spreader of that famous bovine barnyard product which he spreads very quickly and deeply. But we now find that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been engaging in the same game.
Before his trip to Washington to prepare for the summit, the Toronto Star of July 10 had this to say:
I think the Minister of Finance (Allan MacEachen) has made it clear that we think that real interest rates are far too high.
I am not sure whether the Minister of Finance has said that, but apparently the Prime Minister thinks that. The article also reads:
He was expected to ask Reagan today when his interest-rate policy is going to work.
The article went on to say:
It was the first time Trudeau spelled out Canada's position on the contentious economic issue.
And, later:
But although interest rates "are far too high" Trudeau said he would not start an argument with Reagan at the summit meeting.
This is another indication of the solution to the high interest rate problem. The Minister of Agriculture provides his assessment, and his solution was an amendment to the Bank Act, which we have just finished amending.
Then the Prime Minister engages in another strategy, which is hope. He made it very clear he hopes the U.S. strategy will work because we do not seem to have any strategy in Canada that will deal with the problem of high interest rates.
The Prime Minister's commitment is not particularly strong, however, as he is quoted in the press as saying, that although interest rates are far too high, he would not start an argument with Reagan at the summit meeting. The summit is reserved for important issues, yet the most important issue raised by the Prime Minister, according to the press report, was high interest rates.
I am not satisfied with the replies we have been getting from the government, Mr. Speaker. Members of the government are creating an expectation of action with a clearly stated intention in the House by the finance minister of doing nothing.
I have outlined to the House the statement made to the Prime Minister prior to his talks with President Reagan. I . have reviewed the promises made by the Minister of Agriculture to amend the Bank Act when he knows and we know that the Bank Act was amended just seven months ago. Where was the minister with his proposals seven or eight months ago when the Bank Act was open for amendment? Why did he not support some of the amendments that my colleagues offered to regulate interest rate and to regulate the bank spread? He was strangely silent when he could have been taking action. I think the people of Canada deserve to know what the real interest rate policy of the government is, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANK ACT-QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE REVISIONS TO CONTROL INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
There are important reasons why the government is not prepared to contemplate direct control over the interest rates paid or charged by the chartered banks.
First of all, in the context of over-all monetary and exchange rate policy, variable interest rates are an essential part of the mechanism for moderating extreme variations in demand, production, prices and the exchange rate. The fixing of interest rates would tend to result in greater instability in these other important variables. As we know, the current high level of interest rates reflects to a considerable extent the current and expected levels of inflation, as well as current events in the United States and the tightening of monetary policy in an attempt to bring inflation under control. To fix interest rates at an artificially low level in these circumstances would discourage savings and encourage borrowing, thus exacerbating the demand supply pressures and would undoubtedly lead to economic inefficiencies and a worsening of inflation.
July 14, 1981

A second, equally important, aspect of the government's interest rate policies is that connected with the over-all efficiency of the financial system to gather and allocate savings. In this setting, it has generally been government policy to leave interest rates free to be determined by the forces of supply and demand. The rationale for this approach has been that the market mechanism is more finely tuned and tends to allocate resources over all more efficiently than government directives. Also, if the government were involved in the rate-setting business, it would have to be certain that the structure of rates were appropriate, and that the spreads allowed the banks were adequate to meet their capital needs and to provide an adequate return to shareholders. Further, it would be grossly inequitable to control the interest rates paid and charged by the banks without also imposing similar controls on competing institutions and other supplies of credit in the market place.
Adjournment Debate
Furthermore, the imposition of interest rate ceilings on particular categories of loans could result in a drying up of the supply of funds being made for that purpose. Financial institutions, as other corporations, cannot be expected to lend out funds to customers at rates of interest below the level which they must pay to gather those funds from savers in the system and to cover the credit risks and administration costs associated with their lending and borrowing operation.
In addition, it has not been the policy of the government to implement measures to provide broadly based relief from the effects of high interest rates to specific sectors of the economy.
